text.p: The following are some of the leading stories in Finnish papers this morning.
HELSINGIN SANOMAT
- Finns' strong desire for coffee adds 0.1 percent to annual inflation.
- Finns have changed stance towards forestry industry and no longer see logging and environmental protection as contradictory, study by the Finnish Forest Federation says.
- Finlands Bank has not found any proof from achives that it ordered luxury wines found by Swedes in old shipwreck off coastal town of Rauma. @
- Finnish television started broadcasting programmes by satellite to middle and southern Europe.
- Finns consume more allergy medicines than before, worth 200 million markka yearly.
KAUPPALEHTI

- A moderate pay deal for 1998 is most important, whether or not it is centralised is less essential, says Jussi Mustonen, head of economic policy at Confederation of Finnish Industry and Employers (TT), adding he does not see any signs of overheating in economy. @

- Effects of EU integration on Finnish social security system should be studied before deciding whether to join European monetary and economic union (EMU), says director at the Central Organisation of Finnish Trade Unions (SAK).
- Boat sales have exceeded all expectations and stocks have been sold out, sector representatives say.
AAMULEHTI
- Finnish army plans to start employing soldiers on temporary basis to increase reserves of young leaders, military representative says. @
- Finnish cyclist Joona Laukka has reached the top 20 group in Tour de France.
TURUN SANOMAT
- Low Finnish inflation figures give no reason for a more stringent monetary policy, says Matti Vanhala, board member at the Bank of Finland adding that the situation may change though.
- EMU will play much less significant role for Finnish forestry industry than global market prices, reseachers at Finnish Forestry Reseach Institute (METLA) say in report. @
- No direct correlation has been found between heart diseases and eating animal fat, study shows; this could mean health education may be altered, National Health Institute says.
DEMARI
- Finnish medical industry rejects plans to set two-year waiting period before a drug is acceptable for special compensation, saying it violates patient rights.
HUFVUDSTADSBLADET
- Finns try to press Sweden to guarantee official minority status for the Finnish language in whole Sweden.
-- Nora Hallberg, Helsinki newsroom +358-9-680 50 292
